word:greek-nt:G0070.explanation: Agrypnia means sleeplessness or watchings—the state of staying awake.

word:greek-nt:G0092.explanation: This word means “crime”—an offense or wrongful act that violates what is right. It names the wrongdoing itself rather than the person who commits it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Acts and Revelation, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding passages give each occurrence its particular setting. The word points to conduct that is treated as a real offense and therefore may be brought forward as something requiring judgment or acknowledgment.

word:greek-nt:G0153.explanation: αἰσχυνθήσομαι means to be ashamed or to be put to shame.

word:greek-nt:G0276.explanation: This word means “unchangeable,” describing something that cannot be altered, reversed, or made different. It refers to a settled quality rather than an action: what is unchangeable remains firm and does not shift. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews 6:17–18. The word’s basic sense is therefore one of permanence and stability. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains that the matter being described is fixed and cannot be changed.

word:greek-nt:G0319.explanation: Anagnōrizō means to make known. It can also describe someone making himself known.

word:greek-nt:G0355.explanation: Analō means to destroy or consume.

word:greek-nt:G0467.explanation: Antapodidōmi means to repay or give back in return.

word:greek-nt:G0489.explanation: Antimisthia means recompense: a return or reward given in response to something. It can also describe a penalty received for an error.

word:greek-nt:G0580.explanation: This word refers to deprivation or rejection—the loss, removal, or refusal of something. It is a noun describing an outcome or condition rather than an action by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts and Romans, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains the experience of being deprived of something or being rejected. The related rendering “rejection” confirms this basic sense in one occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G0856.explanation: Aphedrōn means a drain or latrine; here it refers to a latrine.

word:greek-nt:G0904.explanation: “Balak” is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Revelation 2:14. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person designated by the name; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain why Balak is mentioned there. Thus, this word functions as a name, not as a general term.

word:greek-nt:G0948.explanation: Bdelyssomai means to abhor, detest, or loathe. It is used of abhorring idols.

word:greek-nt:G0971.explanation: Biazō means to use force or force one's way. It can also mean to suffer violence.

word:greek-nt:G1147.explanation: Daktylos means a finger or fingers.

word:greek-nt:G1239.explanation: Diadidōmi means to distribute or divide something among others.

word:greek-nt:G1381.explanation: Dokimasia means to put something to the test or examine it. It can also mean to approve what is shown to be excellent.

word:greek-nt:G1406.explanation: Drachme means a drachma, a Greek silver coin.

word:greek-nt:G1550.explanation: This word means “to be completely expended” or “to expend”—to use something up fully or to be spent entirely. It describes complete depletion rather than partial use. As a Greek New Testament word, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 12:15. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense centers on something being used up completely. The related active sense is “to expend,” emphasizing the act of spending or using fully.

word:greek-nt:G1741.explanation: Endoxos describes something glorious. It can also describe someone or something highly esteemed or splendid.

word:greek-nt:G1778.explanation: Entalma means an injunction, ordinance, or precept.

word:greek-nt:G1815.explanation: This word means “resurrection”—the rising of the dead to life again. It names the event or reality of resurrection rather than describing a person, action, or feeling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the resurrection itself: life restored after death.

word:greek-nt:G1859.explanation: Heortē means a feast or festival.

word:greek-nt:G1998.explanation: This word means “to run together,” describing people or things moving toward the same place or converging as a group. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in Mark 9:25. The word focuses on coming together in motion, rather than merely being together after movement has stopped. It is therefore a precise action word for gathering or rushing together, with the surrounding passage determining exactly who or what is moving.

word:greek-nt:G2043.explanation: Ereidō means to stick fast or fix firmly.

word:greek-nt:G2111.explanation: Euthetos means fit, suitable, or useful—something appropriate for a purpose or place. It can describe a person as fit for God’s Kingdom or land producing a suitable crop.

word:greek-nt:G2128.explanation: Eulogētos means blessed and worthy of praise, and it is used only of God.

word:greek-nt:G2164.explanation: Euphoreō means to produce abundantly or yield a good harvest, as ground that brings forth plentifully.

word:greek-nt:G2227.explanation: Zōiopoieō means to make alive—to cause the dead to live.

word:greek-nt:G2322.explanation: This word means “service”—work performed for the benefit or care of others. It refers to practical activity carried out on someone’s behalf rather than merely an inward attitude or intention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, so its meaning is concise and focused rather than broadly represented across many passages. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:greek-nt:G2472.explanation: This word describes something regarded as precious—highly valued and of equal worth. In the New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Peter 1:1, and its ordinary sense identifies what is valued rather than disregarded. The wording can stress preciousness itself or parity of value: something is “as precious as” something else, or “equally valuable.” The surrounding verse determines what is being compared or honored.

word:greek-nt:G2490.explanation: Joanan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 3:27, within the genealogy of Jesus. English Bibles render it as “Joanan” or “Joannan.” The available information identifies the person by name, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the name’s meaning. Its precise significance in Luke 3:27 therefore comes from the genealogy and its surrounding context.

word:greek-nt:G2546.explanation: Kakei means “and there,” “there also,” or “yonder,” referring to a place.

word:greek-nt:G2609.explanation: Katagō means to lead down or bring down. It can also describe bringing boats to land.

word:greek-nt:G2645.explanation: Kataloipos refers to what is left—the rest or remainder.

word:greek-nt:G2933.explanation: Ktēma means a possession or piece of property.

word:greek-nt:G3066.explanation: Lucius is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, once in Acts 13:1 and once in Romans 16:21. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person identified by it; the surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which Lucius is intended in each passage. The English rendering preserves the name as “Lucius.”

word:greek-nt:G3394.explanation: Miasmos means pollution or defilement, describing an act that makes something unclean.

word:greek-nt:G3413.explanation: Michael is a personal name rendered “Michael” in the Greek New Testament. It identifies a named figure rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. The name occurs twice in this corpus: once in Jude 1:9 and once in Revelation 12:7. Its basic lexical function is therefore identification—pointing to Michael by name. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain what Michael is doing or how he is presented in either passage.

word:greek-nt:G3624.explanation: Oikos means a house, the material building. It can also refer to a household—the people associated with a home.

word:greek-nt:G3651.explanation: This word means “wholly” or “through and through,” describing something as complete in every part rather than partial or limited. It emphasizes entirety and full extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Its exact force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning points to something complete throughout. The two glosses together show that the word stresses fullness from one end or aspect to another, not merely a large degree or approximate completeness.

word:greek-nt:G3668.explanation: Homoios means likewise, in the same way, or similarly.

word:greek-nt:G3736.explanation: Orysso means to dig, dig out, or excavate.

word:greek-nt:G3783.explanation: This word means “debt”: something owed by one person to another. It can describe an obligation that remains unpaid and therefore is due. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Matthew 6:12 and Romans 4:4. Its basic sense is the amount or obligation owed, while the surrounding verse determines how that idea is applied. The word’s meaning is therefore straightforward: a debt is something a person is responsible to pay or settle.

word:greek-nt:G3840.explanation: Pantothen means from all sides or from every direction.

word:greek-nt:G3905.explanation: Parateinō means to extend, prolong, or continue.

word:greek-nt:G3949.explanation: Parorgizō means to anger or exasperate.

word:greek-nt:G4283.explanation: Proeuangelizomai means to announce the gospel beforehand.

word:greek-nt:G4324.explanation: This word describes threatening someone further—continuing or adding to a threat already made. It is a verb expressing a repeated or intensified act of warning harm or punishment, rather than a general feeling of anger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 4:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of threatening again or further.

word:greek-nt:G4351.explanation: Proskylio means to roll something to or up against a place.

word:greek-nt:G4368.explanation: Prostatis means a female guardian, protector, or patroness. It describes a woman who was a helper of many.

word:greek-nt:G4694.explanation: This Greek New Testament word refers either to a blemish—something marred or defective—or to a reef, a hidden hazard in the sea. These two meanings are distinct, so the surrounding wording determines which sense is intended. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Jude 1:12. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, its precise sense there cannot be stated more narrowly, but its basic meaning points to either a defect or a dangerous obstruction.

word:greek-nt:G4777.explanation: This word means “to suffer together with” or “to suffer with.” It describes sharing in another person’s hardship rather than facing difficulty entirely alone. As a verb, it expresses joining someone in suffering, endurance, or costly service. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Timothy. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains united participation in suffering with another person.

word:greek-nt:G4799.explanation: This word describes confusion or uproar—a condition in which order is disturbed and people or circumstances become unsettled. It points to disorder rather than a calm, organized situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a state of confusion or tumult. The word’s two closely related meanings emphasize both inner disorder and the outward commotion that can result from it.

word:greek-nt:G4801.explanation: Syzeugnymi means to join together or unite.

word:greek-nt:G4838.explanation: Symparalambanō means to take along as a companion.

word:greek-nt:G4874.explanation: Συναναμίγνυσθαι means to mingle with or keep company with.

word:greek-nt:G4957.explanation: Systaurō means to be crucified with another.

word:greek-nt:G5169.explanation: Trypēma means a hole, including the eye of a needle.

word:greek-nt:G5187.explanation: This word means “be conceited”: to have an excessively high view of oneself. It describes a person whose thoughts and attitude are lifted up by self-importance rather than marked by humility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Paul’s letters to Timothy. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding sentence shows how that conceited attitude functions in context.

word:greek-nt:G5248.explanation: Hyperperisseuo means to abound exceedingly or overflow.

word:greek-nt:G5271.explanation: Hypokrinomai means to pretend or act a part.

word:greek-nt:G5518.explanation: Choinix means a dry measure of about 1.92 pints. It is used for measuring wheat and barley.

word:greek-nt:G5521.explanation: Cholē means gall, a bitter substance.

word:greek-nt:G5554.explanation: Chrysodaktylios means adorned with a gold ring.

word:greek-nt:G6029.explanation: This word means “emphatically” or “exceedingly,” intensifying the force of what is being said. It functions as an adverb, showing that an action, statement, or feeling is expressed with especially strong emphasis or to an extraordinary degree. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 14:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense is clear: it strengthens the expression rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself.
